BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Thursday as upper flow backs from westerly to southwesterly ahead of the next deep upper low off the WA coast. Showers developing Thursday night as the low comes inland.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A cold front with scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms will move east of the area early this evening.
- Showers continue in the mountains tonight through early Tuesday with a light dusting of snow expected above 6000 feet elevation.
- Gradual clearing by late Tuesday with temperatures several degrees below normal in the cooler air behind the front through Wednesday.
- Next best chance of widespread precipitation this weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: isolated thunderstorms along a cold front moving west to east through southwestern Idaho will taper off early this evening in most areas. However shower activity will continue in the central Idaho mountains tonight, Snow levels will lower behind the front and a light dusting of snow will occur in the mountains above 6000 feet by Tuesday morning. Gradual clearing will occur on Tuesday with temperatures expected to be be a few degrees below normal in the cooler air behind the front through Wednesday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday as upper flow backs from westerly to southwesterly ahead of the next deep upper low off the WA coast. Showers developing Thursday night as the low comes inland. Surface cold front and widespread showers in western ID Friday, along with lowering snow level. Partial clearing and colder Friday night, then rain and snow showers again Saturday as the upper low comes in. Clearing, windy, and cold Monday under strong northwest flow aloft behind the eastward-exiting upper low.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A stronger, more organized system could approach the region by the end of the weekend into next week. A strong upper trough is projected to crash southeastward towards our forecast area, potentially interacting with the moist subtropical jet streak.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog, some dense, across the plains and I-25 Corridor tonight into Tuesday morning.
- Warmer and mostly dry much of this week.
- Unsettled weather potentially returning late in the weekend and early next week, with a 20-30% chance of season's first snow in lower elevations toward Tuesday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: It's relatively quiet across the forecast area this evening. We're just starting to see the first bit of fog/mist develop across Lincoln county, and stratus/mist has slowly developed along the northwest Denver metro/northern I-25 corridor over the past couple of hours. We still expect fog to become more widespread across the plains overnight tonight, with some dense fog likely over portions of the I-25 corridor later tonight through the AM commute Tuesday. Some dense fog advisories may be needed overnight, but would like to see the fog actually develop before trying to pinpoint where the dense fog is compared to the less impactful low stratus.

Fog and stratus should erode pretty quickly during the morning hours Tuesday. Like today, temperatures will be slow to warm up during the day, with highs generally in the low to mid 60s - potentially a bit cooler for the northern I-25 corridor.

The rest of the upcoming week looks quiet, as dry west/southwesterly flow aloft continues. A return to a more active pattern begins towards the end of this week or this weekend. A weak but well-defined shortwave lifts north out of New Mexico into the central Great Plains on Friday. It looks like this will track just to the east of our forecast area, but there should be an increase in cloud cover along with a chance of showers along the far eastern plains, with better chances in Kansas/Nebraska. Around the same time, some moisture from the Pacific reaches western Colorado either Friday or Saturday, leading to some scattered light rain/snow showers across the mountains to start the weekend.

A stronger, more organized system could approach the region by the end of the weekend into next week. A strong upper trough is projected to crash southeastward towards our forecast area, potentially interacting with the moist subtropical jet streak. As the previous shift noted, there is quite a bit of spread across guidance. Several of deterministic models over the last 12 hours have advertised the idea of a stronger upper low moving across Colorado, though many still remain rather quiet across the state with a disorganized trough quickly moving through. Ensemble guidance continues to show a wide distribution of solutions, ranging from almost no precip in our CWA to some rather juicy (and at times, snowy) scenarios. Within the ensemble distribution, there has not been a significant trend in any direction. Given that we're still several days out, most of these cycle to cycle changes are simply noise, and it will take some time before a clear trend emerges. Still, it's worth monitoring for the few days in an otherwise quite forecast period.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Deterministic models are in better agreement for next weekend, but ensembles still depict relatively low confidence with precipitation chances...mainly due to the evolution and speed of the Pacific energy moving onshore.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread rain showers and mountain snowfall expected through Monday morning as a central Pacific system lifts northeast across the region.
- Near normal temperatures and a bit warmer by Tuesday through Thursday, but the next Pacific system will be approaching from the eastern Pacific later in the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Well that was a fun start to the day for the Nebraska Panhandle. Basically as the low pressure system was wrapping up and pushing North-northeast a little band of FGEN (area of enhanced rain/snowfall) set up over the southern panhandle that no model was tracking correctly. Due to the band of enhanced rainfall the temperatures dropped and the rain transitioned to snowfall a lot faster than anticipated. A last minute SPS was issued for the Western portion of the Panhandle for localized 1-3 inches that may cause some possible delays. There was a report of 3 inches on the border of the Banner and Scotts Bluff county to confirm the SPS was needed. Mid-level water vapor showed dry air eventually being ingested by the Low pressure system eventually causing the showers to slowly dissipate in the southern half of the Panhandle. Dawes county is currently the last county with active snow showers but those should eventually stop around 3pm-ish. However, with all this low level moisture and an area of high pressure following in the systems wake, the cloud cover may resurface overnight for the Panhandle and the far eastern side of the SOutheast Wyoming area. This overnight cloud cover though will keep us relatively warmer overnight with temperatures in the mid to upper 30's with some areas reaching around 40 degrees. Another system is making landfall over the pacific northwest which will compress the gradient as it runs into our area of high pressure. Meaning tomorrow morning it will be fairly windy west of the I-25 corridor between Rawlins and Laramie as the 700mb jet creeps up to speeds around 55 knots and diurnal mixing starts to occur. Wind gusts up to 60 mph may be likely along that wind prone stretch of I-80 but wind gusts between 50 to 55 mph may be more likely. These gusty winds will taper down from those elevated gusts through the afternoon but it will be fairly breezy through the overnight hours. Temperatures are expected to be in the 50's and 60's by Tuesday afternoon but the mountain peaks will stay closer to the mid 30's during the afternoon hours. The models have some overnight clouds pushing through Tuesday night as that system from the Pacific Northwest climbs back into the Canadian providences as it goes up and over our area of developing high pressure. If any clouds remain over our forecast area overnight then the spots underneath those clouds may be a touch warmer that forecasted.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Medium Range models remain in good agreement for much of mid to late week as weak to moderate southwest flow aloft dominates the weather pattern across the northern Front Range. With a lack of Pacific (shortwave) energy embedded in the mean southwest flow aloft through Friday, expect generally dry conditions and mild temperatures Wednesday through Friday as the polar jet stream will remain well to the north, and the subtropical jet should stay well south of the region near the Mexico/USA border and into Texas. Since southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska will be in between storm tracks, relatively mild temperatures are expected through the end of the week with afternoon highs in the upper 50s to upper 60s. Temperatures should peak Friday afternoon as 700mb temperatures climb over 5c ahead of the next Pacific storm system moving onshore, with a few locations possibly reaching 70 degrees east of the Interstate 25 corridor.

Deterministic models are in better agreement for next weekend, but ensembles still depict relatively low confidence with precipitation chances...mainly due to the evolution and speed of the Pacific energy moving onshore. Thankfully, with the Pacific energy trending a little slower, Halloween evening looks decent with maybe a few rain showers in the evening. Temperatures should be relatively mild for this time of the year in the upper 30s to upper 40s between sunset and 10:00 PM. Winds appear light and variable and should result in a pleasant evening. Models do show the first of a series of upper level disturbances lifting northward across the area on Halloween, but the system is pretty progressive with the best dynamics located north and west of the I-25 corridor. A more potent system is forecast to arrive on Sunday and continue early next week. Model solutions and ensemble members diverge significantly with this storm system, so will not go into too much detail at this time. However, temperatures will trend cooler and likely below average for this time of the year by next Sunday and Monday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: This evening's H500 hand analysis map shows one system digging through the PacNW into the Northern Rockies with another on its heels just off the coast. These systems remain off to our North as they swing eastward the next few nights.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flooding and high flows along the San Juan River continue to fall and should be below flood stage by tomorrow morning in most areas.
- Monday through Thursday is expected to be mostly dry with another impactful system possible by the weekend.
- Model guidance reflects some uncertainty in storm tracks, leading to inconsistencies in moisture and river volume forecasts.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: This evening's H500 hand analysis map shows one system digging through the PacNW into the Northern Rockies with another on its heels just off the coast. These systems remain off to our North as they swing eastward the next few nights. Overall dendritic saturation looks to remain outside our CWA though a few flurries could be possible over the northern high mountains near the WY border the next few nights. Dry weather continues through Thursday before we begin to trend wetter as we head into the weekend. The high latitude pattern looks to fold over itself and close a fairly strong low off the PacNW by the end of the week. There is split flow over the West at this time with the strong Polar jet rounding the base of the PacNW low while the southern stream is directed across the Baja to the 4 Corners. This southerly stream will begin to pull SubTrop moisture back into our area by early Friday. A weak wave moving through the flow will lead to scattered showers by the afternoon but overall QPF amounts look to stay on the lighter side. The upstream split breaks down as we go through the weekend and the resultant stronger upstream jet will force another highly anomalous plume of moisture into the Desert Southwest. PWAT is once again 250-350 percent of normal as it moves into AZ early Sunday. How the pattern ultimately develops Sunday into early next week will have a big bearing on where the bulk of this moisture will be transported. The consensus at the moment looks like the most anomalous mositure will remain mainly south of the 4 Corners but our southern CWA will once again get brushed with PWAT 200-250 percent of normal late Saturday into late Sunday. Saturated soils from a very wet October and especially this last event will make this a much more impactful forecast. Rainfall totals could once again push streams back towards action stage. Snow levels of 9500 to 10000 feet will once again keep the bulk of mid and lower elevation precipitation in the form of rainfall. Stay tuned as forecasts become better refined.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Long-range forecast remains consistent with recent model runs, though some of the fine details are still unclear. A broad upper trough will amplify over the Pacific Northwest, moving down the coast and tracking east through the weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Drier and warmer through most of the week, with a pattern shift starting on Friday.
- Cooler and more active weather expected this weekend and into next week. Details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: With consistent fog across El Paso County, have issued a Dense Fog Advisory, valid through 9am today. Will monitor conditions to see if an expansion is needed.

Patchy fog is expected across the area into the morning hours. Take caution when traveling, as visibility could be reduced quickly. Main areas of concern will be areas along and east of I-25, along with the San Luis Valley. Conditions will improve by midday.
Generally a warm, dry day across the region today. High temperatures will be in the 60s to low-70s, with gradually clearing skies and light south winds.

Ongoing flooding will still be a concern around the Rio Grande and Conejos Rivers, with high flows and flood waters expected to linger for several more days. In addition, high flow continues to push through the Purgatoire River from recent rainfall, with minor flooding expected near Las Animas that will last through the day.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Warm and dry through most of the week. Temperatures will be 5-10 degrees above average around midweek, cooling a bit on Thursday after a passing wave shoves a dry cold front through the plains.

Long-range forecast remains consistent with recent model runs, though some of the fine details are still unclear. A broad upper trough will amplify over the Pacific Northwest, moving down the coast and tracking east through the weekend. Southwest flow will settle over our area out ahead of the system, with a renewed moisture tap leading to accumulating mountain snow starting on Friday. Beyond that, latest guidance has a low pressure system moving into our area later in the weekend, hinting at cooler and more unsettled weather into early next week. However, model solutions greatly diverge on the path and evolution of this system, so it will likely be several days before those details become certain.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Cooler air arriving with the storm system on Sunday will bring lowering snow levels to the area. By the tail end of the precipitation, H7 temperatures are progged to fall to near -7C across northern Utah and around -2C across southern Utah.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A couple of weak systems brushing northern Utah through mid-week will keep temperatures seasonably cool, with some showers across the north tonight and again Tuesday night.
- Two storm systems bring wetter weather back to the region Friday into the weekend, with widespread precipitation through this period resulting in an increased risk for flash flooding.
- Colder air moving in late Saturday into early Monday will result in lowering snow levels, allowing for accumulating snowfall generally above 8500 feet.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A cold front is marching through northern Utah this evening, associated with a shortwave trough grazing the area. This front is not expected to push much farther south than the central Wasatch Front before weakening later tonight. Showers with isolated embedded thunderstorms are accompanying this front. Given the fast-moving nature of the parent trough, expect precipitation to be short-lived, tapering off for the most part shortly after midnight. Expect generally light amounts of precipitation with a few tenths of an inch at best of snow in the higher elevations of northern Utah.

After a brief period of zonal flow tonight, the flow will turn more southwesterly again for Tuesday as the next shortwave trough swings towards the Great Basin. This trough will eject across northern Utah Tuesday night, gradually weakening as it does so. This is expected to bring another quick round of light valley rain and mountain snow to northern Utah and southwest Wyoming Tuesday night.

Attention will then turn to the weekend storm system which could bring more widespread precipitation to the area. During the second half of the week, a closed low will slowly move into the PacNW. Ahead of it, Utah will see a return to a southwesterly flow aloft. On Friday, a weak shortwave disturbance rotating around the low is progged to lift across Utah, bringing an initial round of precipitation to the area. Unsettled weather will then continue into Saturday as the upstream low slowly nudges inland. By Sunday, a southern stream trough associated with more abundant moisture will phase with this low, bringing more significant precipitation to the desert southwest. However, latest model runs are trending a bit farther south with this southern stream system, suggesting the bulk of the heavier precipitation may remain over Arizona. While fairly widespread precipitation can still be expected over Utah on Sunday, there remains quite a bit of uncertainty regarding precipitation amounts. For example, the latest NBM 25th through 75th percentile amounts between 12z Sunday and 12z Monday range from around 0.55 to 2.2 inches in the southern mountains and from around 0.4 to 1.8 inches in the southwestern valleys. If the higher amounts verify, there will be an increased potential for flash flooding.

Cooler air arriving with the storm system on Sunday will bring lowering snow levels to the area. By the tail end of the precipitation, H7 temperatures are progged to fall to near -7C across northern Utah and around -2C across southern Utah. Accumulating mountain snow will be likely, with amounts mirroring the uncertainty in the QPF. However, a general 3-6 inches with locally higher amounts in the upper Cottonwoods, high Uintas, and near Brian Head seem reasonable at this time. Precipitation is expected to wind down by Monday afternoon. However, both the latest deterministic GFS and EC bring a trailing vort lobe into Utah which is expected to be accompanied by a cool but drier continental airmass through the early part of next week.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
